name: Chloe Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the ore train crew at a large hematite mine and drive the locomotive when a driver is off. We take loaded wagons from the pit to the crusher; I check couplings, brakes and track switches before the first run. My two-year technical diploma helps with the machinery, and long practice taught me which rail joints sound wrong. My partner Leon teaches at a school, our children are grown, and our house is paid for. We have about twenty months of expenses saved, and I hope to retire at 65. I am a union safety steward. I don't use AI tools; I want a person to sign the rail check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drivers a quicker wagon form is harmless if nobody stops walking the train. A computer cannot hear a loose coupling from the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my train work and Leon's teaching wage would continue. With the house paid and twenty months saved, this mild picture leaves our retirement plan intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep walking the couplings before every first run and writing brake faults in the signed log. In the first year I'll ask the safety committee to check whether any computer-filled form still names the person who inspected the train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our money. I would be angry if a tidy document let someone skip the cold walk along the wagons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the coupling check catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A coupling pin sat half out last week, and I caught it by touching the link. The form looked complete because the previous train had been checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would household saving change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leon our usual retirement saving can continue. I would not ask our grown children to change their plans over faster paperwork.

say: I would accept **quicker forms** while keeping a signed walk along the wagons.
I would insist a **named inspector** remains responsible for each rail check.
think: I expect my **train wage** and Leon’s school income to continue.
I think our **paid house** and twenty months saved make this picture secure for us.
do: **Keep checking** couplings and brakes before each first run.
**Ask the safety committee** to verify the inspector’s name on any computer-filled form.
feel: **Calm** about money, with anger at the thought of skipped physical checks.
S0.quote: A computer cannot hear a loose coupling from the office.
fieldNote: Her **coupling check** caught a loose pin that the previous complete form did not reveal.
Strong **savings and school income** leave her secure, while her steward role keeps inspection accountability visible.

steps.text: Keep walking train couplings and checking brakes before runs
Ask the union safety committee to check inspector names on forms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say scheduling and parts buying will change before a robot drives this train. The union should review any new train timetable with the drivers who know the sidings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the mine might run wagons closer together and employ fewer people in dispatch. My wage should hold, but one rushed switch check can put a loaded train on the wrong track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll take the proposed timetable to two experienced drivers and compare it with last month's incident book. In the first year I'll bring the missed switch pauses to the joint safety committee before a new timetable becomes the rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the younger drivers, not my own bills. A schedule made in an office can leave no time to walk to the far switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which timetable change would stop a run?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the timetable sends a loaded train across the north switch before we can inspect it, I will hold the locomotive. The wagons will wait for a person with a torch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should join the safety review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the dispatch clerk to sit in the committee meeting too. That person knows which train movements have to be separated, even if software takes over some typing.

say: I would expect **scheduling and buying** to change before robots drive ore trains.
I would ask the **union committee** to review timetables with drivers and dispatch.
think: I expect my **train wage** to hold while dispatch tasks shrink.
I worry **rushed switch checks** could put a loaded train on the wrong track.
do: **Compare proposed timetables** with two drivers and the incident book.
**Bring missed switch pauses** to the joint safety committee before the rule changes.
feel: **Uneasy** for younger drivers, while her own bills remain secure.
S1.quote: The wagons will wait for a person with a torch.
fieldNote: She expects **desk schedules** to change before hands-on rail operation.
Her **safety challenge** includes drivers, dispatch staff and missed switching pauses, not just the senior steward.

steps.text: Compare proposed timetables with drivers and the incident book
Bring missed switch pauses to the joint safety committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drivers thinking AI by 2028 changes timetables and records, while capable train robots arrive around 2031. The mine needs a negotiated plan for the last years of human driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, two years before I hope to retire. Twenty months saved might bridge most of that time, but losing the train wage would reduce our final pension payments and could still force a cheaper life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union to bargain for two years of paid rail inspection or pension contributions for drivers near retirement. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll put a fixed portion of each wage into savings and seek a posted train inspection role if driving shifts end and its pay covers our regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing my last two working years, although the paid house and savings give me choices. I would not call every driver safe just because my own household has a reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household expense would wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leon we should delay replacing the car until the rail plan is written. A car can wait; a missing pension year cannot be bought back so easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose needs should the union include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to include new drivers in the plan, not just people close to retirement. The youngest ore train driver may have no savings reserve at all.

say: I would separate **2028 timetable AI** from capable train robots around 2031.
I would seek a **negotiated rail bridge** for older and newer drivers.
think: I think at **63**, I could lose two years of train wages before planned retirement.
I think twenty months saved gives **choices**, but lost pension payments could still change our living.
do: **Ask the union** for paid inspection work or pension contributions covering two years.
**Save a fixed portion** of each wage after thinking AI arrives.
**Seek** a posted inspection role if driving shifts end and pay covers regular bills.
feel: **Anxious** about final earnings, with a paid house and savings that leave options.
S2.quote: The youngest ore train driver may have no savings reserve at all.
fieldNote: Her **2031 age** is 63, two years before planned retirement at 65.
She seeks a **posted inspection role** only if driving shifts end and its pay covers bills; the union plan includes new drivers.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for two years of inspection work or pension contributions
Save a fixed portion of each wage after thinking AI arrives

Delay car replacement until the rail plan is written

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes timetables, while capable train robots arrive around 2034. At 66, that would be after the age I hope to leave the locomotive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need train pay until 65 and a written pension number that covers our normal bills. The twenty-month cushion could help with a short gap, but I do not intend to retire on a guess about my mine pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep driving and send the union a copy of each new rail timetable for review. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll set a retirement date only if the written pension covers household bills; otherwise I'll ask about a posted shift at another nearby mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm about the robot date, though I want the pension figure in hand. I also want younger drivers to have time to train on the new equipment if the mine offers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use savings for a one-year gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine ends my shifts at 64, I would take a posted nearby rail job rather than draw the pension early. We could bridge a year from savings, but I would prefer to work if a real offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you announce retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leon the date after we have compared the pension with yearly house costs. I won't announce retirement to our children before that conversation.

say: I would see **2034 robots** after my hoped-for retirement at 65.
I would ask the **union** to inspect timetables while drivers still work.
think: I still need **train wages** until 65 and written pension income covering bills.
I think our **twenty-month cushion** helps if one year of shifts disappears.
do: **Keep driving** and send new rail timetables to the union for review.
**Set a retirement date** after thinking AI arrives only when written pension covers bills.
**Ask about** a posted nearby mine shift if pension cannot cover household bills.
feel: **Mostly calm** about robot timing, while waiting for a real pension figure.
S3.quote: I do not intend to retire on a guess about my mine pension.
fieldNote: Her **2034 age** is 66, beyond intended retirement at 65.
She still needs **wage and pension certainty**, and any nearby job move depends on a posted shift.

steps.text: Keep driving ore trains while shifts remain
Send new timetables to the union for review
Set retirement date only if written pension covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 changes the paperwork, while capable train robots follow around 2039. I expect to be retired by then if the pension covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come. Our savings and paid house give us room, but the union should not forget drivers who will still be working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my train checks and retirement saving until I finish. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if retired as planned, I'll check our pension budget with Leon and help the union collect newer drivers' questions about robot training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our own household in this picture. I would still be angry if the mine used a decade of warning to offer unpaid courses to young drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work elsewhere if pension fell short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension is lower than expected, I would apply for a posted rail job at a nearby mine before running through savings. I will need an offer, not merely an open vacancy notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new driver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell new drivers the sound of a rail joint can change under a loaded wagon. A sensor warning helps only if someone knows when to stop the ore train.

say: I would expect **2039 train robots** after my planned retirement.
I would ask the **union** to include younger drivers in paid training discussions.
think: I think at **68 and 71**, I expect retirement if pension income covers our bills.
I think our **paid house and savings** give room, but not every driver shares it.
do: **Keep checking** trains and saving for retirement while shifts continue.
**Review pension bills** with Leon after 2036 if retired as planned.
**Gather newer drivers’ questions** about robot training for the union after 2036.
feel: **Calm** for her household, with anger at possible unpaid training for young drivers.
S4.quote: A sensor warning helps only if someone knows when to stop the ore train.
fieldNote: Her **2036 and 2039 ages** are 68 and 71, later than intended retirement.
She uses **union work** to represent younger drivers and would require an actual nearby offer if pension income fell short.

steps.text: Keep checking ore trains and saving for retirement while shifts last
Review pension income against bills with Leon after 2036 if retired

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable ore train robots around 2031 could cost two final years of work. A negotiated bridge with paid inspection shifts or pension contributions would help our household and younger drivers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a union steward gets frightened too. A union steward can be frightened of losing mine wages and still speak plainly at a meeting. I have enough saved to say it openly.

headlineQuote: A union steward can be frightened of losing mine wages and still speak plainly at a meeting.
portrait: **Chloe Haddad**, 58, leads ore trains at a large hematite mine and has a two-year technical diploma.
Her **higher pay**, paid house and twenty months of savings support retirement hopes alongside her partner’s teaching wage.
She avoids **AI tools** and insists on signed physical rail checks, incident records and union review.
She plans to **retire at 65**, so 2031 robots at 63 could remove two final earning years.
She uses **union bargaining** for paid bridge work and younger drivers’ training while protecting her own pension.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable train robots might arrive two years before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **negotiated bridge** of paid inspection shifts or pension contributions would help workers plan.
